common_name: Souvenir du Docteur Jamain Rose (Deep Maroon Shade-Tolerant Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; this 1865 hybrid perpetual tolerates more shade than most roses and benefits from some afternoon relief from harsh sun, which can scorch its dark petals.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Souvenir du Docteur Jamain, introduced in 1865, bears deep maroon-purple double flowers with an intensely rich, old-rose fragrance considered among the strongest of any antique rose. Its dark petals are prone to sunburn and browning in intense afternoon sun, so a site with some relief from the harshest exposure — such as filtered light or morning sun with afternoon shade — actually improves flower quality, making it one of the more shade-tolerant heirloom roses available. It grows into a tall, somewhat lax shrub that can be trained as a short climber, and reblooms through the season with reasonable reliability for a Victorian-era hybrid perpetual. Prune lightly after each flowering flush and remove dead or crossing wood in late winter.

common_name: Climbing Cecile Brunner Rose (Extremely Vigorous Sweetheart Climbing Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring against a large, sturdy structure — this climbing sport of the bush Cecile Brunner is exceptionally vigorous and can scramble 20-30 feet into a tree or over an arbor if left unchecked.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, siting it at the base of a large, sturdy pergola, fence, or tree, since this climbing sport of the famous 1881 Sweetheart Rose is dramatically more vigorous than the compact bush form and needs substantial room and support to look its best. It bears the same small, perfectly formed, high-centered pale pink buds prized for boutonnieres and posies, opening to lightly fragrant flowers in a spectacular once-yearly spring flush so heavy it can cover the entire structure in bloom. Give it several years to establish before expecting its full mature size, and prune only to remove dead wood and control reach, since it blooms mainly on old wood and heavy pruning sacrifices the following spring's display.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Complicata is an unusually vigorous, large-growing Gallica-type rose, often trained as a short climber or left to form a big informal shrub.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Complicata produces large, single, clear pink flowers with a bright white eye and prominent golden stamens, a bold, simple flower form that stands in contrast to the densely petaled doubles typical of most old garden roses, and its blooms are large enough to rival modern hybrid teas despite the plant's antique parentage. It flowers in one spectacular, heavy spring flush, covering its arching canes so thoroughly the foliage nearly disappears, then rests for the remainder of the season like other once-blooming Gallica-type roses. Its unusually vigorous, large habit suits it to a big informal shrub border or training as a short climber on a fence or arbor. It is exceptionally tough, disease-resistant, and cold-hardy, needing only removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Ballerina Rose (Single Pink Hybrid Musk with White Eye)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall in full sun to part shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Ballerina is a 1937 English hybrid musk grown for huge clusters of small single flowers rather than large individual blooms.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants to allow for a broad, rounded habit. Ballerina, introduced in England in 1937, is a hybrid musk rose famous for its enormous, hydrangea-like clusters of small, single, soft pink flowers with a white eye, giving an airy, almost floral-bouquet effect very different from the large individual blooms of hybrid tea roses. As a hybrid musk it tolerates more shade than most roses, flowering respectably with only four to five hours of direct sun, and it blooms nearly continuously from late spring through fall with minimal deadheading needed, since spent flower clusters are inconspicuous. It shows good disease resistance and needs only a light pruning in late winter to shape the plant and remove old, unproductive wood.
sources: American Rose Society — Hybrid Musk Rose Class Descriptions

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall in full sun to part shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Cornelia is a 1925 English hybrid musk with a lax, arching habit that can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a short climber.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Cornelia, a hybrid musk rose from 1925, bears large clusters of small, semi-double flowers in a warm blend of apricot, coral, and pink that fades to a softer pink as blooms age, carrying the characteristic sweet musk fragrance of the class. It flowers in strong flushes from late spring through fall, and its lax, arching canes can be grown as a large informal shrub or trained against a wall or fence as a short climber. As a hybrid musk it tolerates more shade than most roses, performing well with four to five hours of direct sun, and shows good resistance to blackspot. Prune back by about a third in late winter if grown as a shrub, or simply remove old wood if trained as a climber.
sources: American Rose Society — Hybrid Musk Rose Class Descriptions

common_name: Penelope Rose (Creamy Apricot-Pink Fragrant Hybrid Musk)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall in full sun to part shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Penelope is a 1924 English hybrid musk valued for fragrant clustered flowers and attractive coral-pink hips in fall.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Penelope, one of the earliest and most celebrated hybrid musk roses, bears large clusters of semi-double flowers opening pale apricot-pink and fading to a soft creamy blush, with a strong, sweet musk fragrance that carries well through the garden. If flowers are left unspent rather than deadheaded, it develops attractive coral-pink hips in fall that extend its ornamental season and provide food for birds. As a hybrid musk it tolerates more shade than most roses, blooming well with four to five hours of direct sun, and its bushy, rounded habit works as a specimen shrub or informal hedge. Prune back by about a third in late winter to maintain a full, well-branched shape.
sources: American Rose Society — Hybrid Musk Rose Class Descriptions
